267.title: Kara: the steel circle
267.hook: a steel bracelet, a circle without end, reminding the hand what it's for
267.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the five Ks wear a plain steel or iron kara on the wrist, and other Sikhs often wear one too, as a constant reminder of the Guru and of what their hands should do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kangha, the small comb: clean and ordered. Today, the K you've most likely already seen, on a wrist at the next desk.

Some people tie a string around a finger so they won't forget something. Others write a word on the back of their hand. The trick works because hands are always in view: typing, reaching, holding a cup, holding a phone. Want a reminder you'll see a hundred times a day? Put it on your hand. Sikhs keep one there too: a plain circle of steel at the wrist. Today, the third of the five Ks: kara.
screen: `A STRING ON A FINGER.` → `HANDS, ALWAYS IN VIEW.` → `A STEEL CIRCLE AT THE WRIST.`

segments.voice: Kara means a bracelet, and the Sikh kara is a very particular one: plain steel or iron, no gold, no gems, no decoration. It's worn on the wrist, often the right, or the hand a person uses most. It carries three simple ideas. First, the circle. It has no beginning and no end, and Sikhs often say that's a picture of God, the One without beginning or end, and of the unbroken bond between a Sikh and the Guru. Second, the steel. Not gold, which says wealth, or silver, which says status. Steel is what tools and plows are made of, humble and strong. Rich or poor, a Sikh wears the same kara. Third, the one people remember: the hand. Every time the hand moves, the kara moves with it. Reaching for something that isn't yours, raising a fist in anger, signing a dishonest paper: the steel is right there, catching the light, asking a quiet question. What are these hands doing? It's the same question under the whole rehat. The Gurus taught kirat karni, honest work with your own hands, and seva, service with your own hands. The kara just keeps the question on your wrist. You'll often see it on Sikhs who don't keep all five, and on Punjabi wrists of other backgrounds too. Plain, heavy, cool against the skin, and never quite letting you forget.
screen: `KARA — PLAIN STEEL, NO GOLD.` · `A CIRCLE: NO BEGINNING, NO END.` · `STEEL: HUMBLE, STRONG, THE SAME FOR ALL.` · `ON THE HAND THAT ACTS.` · then, large: `WHAT ARE THESE HANDS DOING.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up, and look at them. Think of what they've done today, what they carried, typed, cooked, held, maybe what they shouldn't have done, with honest looking and no scolding. Then choose one good thing these hands will do before the day ends, and let them rest, open, while you breathe.
Kara. The plain steel bracelet, the third K: a circle without end, the same for rich and poor, reminding the hand what it's for.
Your line: what are these hands doing. The steel asks; the hands answer. That's day two hundred sixty-seven.

268.title: Kachhera: ready and restrained
268.hook: cotton undershorts, a sign of readiness and self-restraint
268.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the five Ks, women and men, wear a kachhera at all times, and they often describe it as a reminder of modesty, self-control and readiness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kara, the steel circle that asks what these hands are doing. Today, the K that nobody sees, and why it's there anyway.

Firefighters sleep near their boots. Some keep their gear laid out so they can step into it in seconds. Nobody at the dinner table sees any of it, but it says something about who they are: I'm ready, if I'm needed. Most of the five Ks can be seen: the hair, the turban over it, the steel at the wrist. One can't. It's worn under everything, every day, and its whole meaning is about what's underneath: readiness, and restraint. Today, the fourth of the five Ks: kachhera.
screen: `BOOTS BY THE BED.` → `UNSEEN, BUT READY.` → `THE K UNDER EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Kachhera is a pair of cotton undershorts, loose, reaching toward the knee, usually tied with a drawstring. Men and women who keep the five Ks both wear it. It sounds like the plainest thing in the world, but it carries two ideas: ready, and restrained. Ready first. In the Gurus' time, a common garment was the dhoti, a long wrapped cloth, which isn't easy to run or ride in. The kachhera is practical: you can move, climb, ride, work in the fields or defend the defenseless at a moment's notice. For the Khalsa, called to be saint-soldiers, readiness mattered. Now restrained. The kachhera is also, very simply, modest. Sikhs speak of it as a reminder of self-control, especially over kaam, desire, the first of the five thieves from four weeks ago. It stands for faithfulness in marriage and dignity in the body. The Rehat Maryada counts adultery among the four things a Sikh must never do, which comes up in two days. And here's the quiet thing: nobody sees it. It's a promise kept when no one's checking, and that's often where character actually lives: not in what's shown, but in what's chosen when nobody would know. Ready to act when someone needs you. Restrained when all you'd be serving is yourself. Both at once, under everything.

segments.voice: Choose one small restraint, the extra scroll, the sharp reply, the second dessert, the purchase you don't need, the glance that doesn't honor someone, and picture holding back calmly, with dignity, not gritted teeth. Then think of one way you could be ready for someone who might need you, and hold both as you breathe.
Kachhera. The cotton undershorts, the fourth K: ready to act, restrained in desire, a promise kept where no one sees.
Your line: ready and restrained. A promise doesn't need to be seen to hold. Day two hundred sixty-eight, done.

269.title: Kirpan: the small sword
269.hook: a small sword, carried as a duty to protect the defenseless
269.howItsDone: Amritdhari Sikhs carry a kirpan at all times in a gatra, often small and worn under clothing, as an article of faith and a reminder of the duty to protect others; Sikh teaching forbids using it in aggression.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kachhera, the K no one sees: ready and restrained. Today, the fifth K, and one that needs care to explain.

Carry it always, and hope never to need it. Not a phone or a first-aid kit, but a blade, worn in a cloth sheath across the body, often small, often under the clothes. Meeting the idea for the first time, that can sound alarming. Sikhs who carry it often describe the opposite: a steadying weight, because of what it stands for and the promise attached to it. Today, the fifth of the five Ks: kirpan.
screen: `CARRY IT ALWAYS.` → `HOPE NEVER TO NEED IT.` → `THE FIFTH K.`

segments.voice: The kirpan is a small sword, worn in a sheath on a cloth strap called a gatra, by Sikhs who have taken amrit. Sikhs hear mercy and honor in its name, which is today's line; the word itself comes back in a few days. Today's question is what it's for. It stands for a duty, not a threat: to protect the defenseless, to stand against injustice, like Kabir's true warrior, the one who fights for the helpless and never leaves the field. Why a sword at all? The Sikh Gurus lived through persecution. Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur were executed by the authorities of their day. Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa as saint-soldiers: saints first, soldiers when they must be. So the kirpan sits beside the kesh, the comb, the steel circle and the kachhera as part of one promise, not a weapon kept for its own sake. Sikh teaching is firm: never for aggression, revenge or show. Drawing it in anger betrays everything it means. A Sikh who carries one may go a whole life without drawing it. Like the kara, it's a reminder. Of mercy. Of honor. Of the people you'd stand in front of.
screen: `KIRPAN — THE SMALL SWORD.` · `A DUTY, NOT A THREAT.` · `SAINTS FIRST, SOLDIERS WHEN THEY MUST.` · `NEVER DRAWN IN ANGER.` · then, large: `MERCY AND HONOR.`

segments.voice: Think about whom you would protect: a child, a parent, a friend, then wider, a neighbor who lives alone, a coworker who gets picked on, someone in your town without a voice. Picture standing beside them, not with a weapon, but with steadiness and care. Ask yourself what protecting them would actually look like this week, and breathe with it.
Kirpan. The small sword, the fifth K: carried as a duty to protect the defenseless, and heard by Sikhs as mercy and honor.
Your line: mercy and honor. Carried always, and hoped never to be needed. See you tomorrow.

270.title: The four things avoided
270.hook: the Rehat Maryada lists cutting hair, tobacco and intoxicants, ritually slaughtered meat, and adultery; diets differ among Sikhs
270.howItsDone: At the amrit ceremony, new initiates are told of the four kurehats from the Sikh Rehat Maryada; gurdwara langar is, by near-universal custom, vegetarian, while Sikhs' own diets vary, from strict vegetarianism to eating jhatka meat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirpan, the small sword: mercy and honor. That's all five Ks. Today, the other side of the rehat: the four things a Sikh who takes amrit promises to avoid.

Most promises have two halves. A doctor's oath says help, and also do no harm. A close friendship has things you always do, show up, tell the truth, and a few things you never do, like reading the other's private messages. The yes gives a life its shape; the no protects it. The Sikh rehat is the same. For five days, the yes: hair kept, a comb, a steel circle, readiness, a sword of mercy. Today, the short list of no's, four of them. Today's word: kurehat.
screen: `EVERY PROMISE HAS TWO HALVES.` → `THE YES GIVES SHAPE.` → `THE NO PROTECTS IT.`

segments.voice: Rehat, remember, is the way of living. Put ku in front, meaning wrong or bad, and you get kurehat: a breach of that way. The Sikh Rehat Maryada names four for Sikhs who have taken amrit. One: cutting or removing the hair, which undoes the kesh. Two: using tobacco. The code also forbids alcohol and other intoxicants, and many Sikhs speak of all of these together: keep the body and mind clear. Three: eating kutha, meat from an animal killed in a ritual way. Four: adultery, a sexual relationship outside one's marriage. Two honest notes, because this is where people often get confused. First, on meat, Sikhs differ. Gurdwara langar is, by near-universal custom, vegetarian, so anyone of any background can eat. Many Sikhs are fully vegetarian. Others eat meat that isn't ritually slaughtered, often called jhatka, killed with a single blow. Many understand the kutha rule as rejecting meat killed as a religious ritual; it's a rule about Sikh practice, not a judgment on neighbors whose faiths keep their own rites. Second, the four aren't a list of sins to be scared of. They're guardrails around the promise of amrit. If someone who has taken amrit breaks one, the tradition doesn't throw them out; it offers a path back, through confession before five Sikhs and taking amrit again. Keep it clean: the hair, the mind, the table, the marriage.

segments.voice: Think of one small no that protects a bigger yes: no second drink, no cigarette, no scrolling late into the night, no flirting with a line you've promised not to cross. Choose one, and picture keeping it this evening, calmly, as a guardrail, not a cage. Then rest with the breath, clear and steady.
Kurehat. A breach of the rehat; the Rehat Maryada names four for Sikhs who've taken amrit: cutting the hair, tobacco, kutha meat and adultery.
Your line: keep it clean. A small no can guard a bigger yes. Two hundred seventy days, and counting.

271.title: Taking amrit
271.hook: the initiation, given by five Sikhs, is a serious personal step, never pressed on anyone
271.howItsDone: Amrit sanchar is held in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib, usually in a gurdwara, where five initiated Sikhs prepare amrit in an iron bowl while reciting five banis; those who take it commit to the five Ks, daily prayer and the Rehat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kurehat: the four things an initiated Sikh avoids. Keep it clean. Today, the ceremony where that promise is made.

A quiet room. Five people standing. A steel bowl of water, and a double-edged sword moving through it slowly. For the person who has come to take amrit, this is a promise thought about for weeks, sometimes years, then said aloud in front of people who matter. Nobody can sign you up for it. Nobody is supposed to push you into it. Today: taking amrit.
screen: `A QUIET ROOM, A STEEL BOWL.` → `A PROMISE SAID ALOUD.` → `NOBODY SIGNS YOU UP.`

segments.voice: Amrit means the nectar of immortality. Sanchar means bringing it into being, passing it on. Together, amrit sanchar is the Sikh initiation, also called khande di pahul, the initiation of the double-edged sword. It goes back to Vaisakhi, 1699, at Anandpur. Guru Gobind Singh stirred water in an iron bowl with a khanda, a double-edged sword. Tradition says Mata Sahib Kaur added sugar puffs, so the steel would carry sweetness too. He gave it to the first five, the panj pyare, the five beloved ones. Then, in the tradition's telling, came the surprise. He asked the five to give it to him. The Guru, with folded hands, received it from the people he had just initiated. Today's ceremony keeps that shape. Five initiated Sikhs, standing in for the panj pyare, prepare the amrit while reciting five prayers from the Sikh daily prayers, including Guru Nanak's Japji. The person taking it drinks from cupped hands, and it's sprinkled on the eyes and the hair. They greet each other: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh. The Khalsa belongs to God, and so does the victory. They're taught the code: the five Ks, the daily prayers, and yesterday's four things avoided. It's a real commitment, and Sikhs treat it that way. People take amrit at different ages: some as teenagers, some in their forties, some never. The Sikh code of conduct says anyone of any background who is ready to live by the vows may take it. The word that matters is ready. Amrit isn't handed out to fill a room. It's a step a person chooses when the promise is theirs.
screen: `AMRIT — THE NECTAR OF IMMORTALITY.` · `ANANDPUR, 1699: THE FIRST FIVE.` · `THE GURU ASKS THE FIVE TO INITIATE HIM.` · `A STEP TAKEN WHEN YOU'RE READY.` · then, large: `A STEP, NOT A PRESSURE.`

segments.voice: Think of one commitment in your life, one you made or one you're still weighing, and ask it three honest questions: is this mine, or am I doing it because someone expects it; what would it ask of me on an ordinary Tuesday; and what would keeping it give back. You don't have to decide anything now; just let the questions sit, the way the five let the water be stirred slowly.
Amrit sanchar. The Sikh initiation, given by five initiated Sikhs, with water stirred by a double-edged sword. A serious step, chosen, never pressed.
Your line: a step, not a pressure. A yes means most when there was room to say not yet. That's day two hundred seventy-one.

272.title: Many ways of being Sikh
272.hook: amritdhari, keshdhari, sahajdhari: people live their Sikhi at many stages, and the Gurus welcomed seekers
272.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of amritdhari (initiated), keshdhari (keeping uncut hair) and sahajdhari Sikhs; gurdwaras welcome everyone to the sangat and the langar, whatever their stage or background.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amrit sanchar, taken when a person is ready: a step, not a pressure. So what about everyone who hasn't taken that step?
screen: `AMRIT SANCHAR — A STEP, NOT A PRESSURE.`

segments.voice: Sunday, the langar hall of a gurdwara, and the row on the floor is a mix. One man wears a tall blue turban and a steel kara, and took amrit years ago. Next to him, his nephew, uncut hair tied under a patka, still thinking about amrit. Across the row, a woman with short hair who sings every hymn by heart. A college student, here with a friend for the first time. Same floor, same food. Today: many ways of being Sikh.
screen: `ONE LANGAR HALL.` → `A TURBAN, A PATKA, SHORT HAIR, A GUEST.` → `ALL ON THE SAME FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Back on day one hundred thirty-nine, at the gurdwara door, the short answer was: start where you are. Today, the words Sikhs use for it. Sikh itself means a learner, a disciple, usually traced to the same old root as the Sanskrit shishya, a student. So the name assumes you're somewhere along the way, not finished. Sikhs often use three words for where people are. Amritdhari: one who has taken amrit and keeps the full discipline. Keshdhari: one who keeps uncut hair but hasn't yet taken amrit. And sahajdhari, usually explained from sahaj, ease or gradualness: one who walks the path at their own pace, often without the outward forms. You'll also hear mona, for a Sikh who cuts their hair. Sikhs don't all agree on how these words should be used. The Sikh code of conduct defines a Sikh by belief: in one God, the ten Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib, and the tenth Guru's amrit. How far the word stretches is a live debate, and in recent decades it has even reached the courts in India. What nobody disputes is where the Gurus began. Guru Nanak sat with anyone. The Guru Granth Sahib includes voices from beyond the Gurus' own line: Muslim and Hindu saints, a weaver, a leatherworker. The langar feeds whoever walks in. The Gurus built a house with an open door. So the everyday question isn't, am I Sikh enough? It's the learner's question: what's my next step? For one person it's amrit. For another, learning to read Gurmukhi. For a guest, maybe just sitting on the floor and eating.
screen: `SIKH MEANS LEARNER.` · `AMRITDHARI, KESHDHARI, SAHAJDHARI.` · `SIKHS DEBATE WHERE THE LINES FALL.` · `THE GURUS KEPT AN OPEN DOOR.` · then, large: `EVERY SEEKER WELCOME.`

segments.voice: Place yourself in that langar hall, exactly as you are today, whatever you believe, whatever you're unsure of. If a voice in you says you're too early, too late or not enough, let it be there, and let it quiet down. Then ask the learner's question gently, what's one next step for me in anything that matters, and hold the answer lightly.
Sahajdhari, one who walks at their own pace. Sikh means learner; amritdhari, keshdhari, sahajdhari: people live their Sikhi at many stages, and the Gurus welcomed seekers.
Your line: every seeker welcome. Sikh means learner, and a learner is never finished. Day two hundred seventy-two, done.

273.title: The written code
273.hook: the Sikh Rehat Maryada, agreed by the panth in the 1940s and published in 1950, sets out the shared code
273.howItsDone: The Sikh Rehat Maryada, published by the SGPC, is used by gurdwaras in India and abroad to guide worship and ceremonies; Sikhs preparing for amrit often read it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many ways of being Sikh: every seeker welcome. Today, the book that holds this whole stretch together.

Every family has rules nobody wrote down. Shoes off at the door. Grandma gets the first plate. Nobody touches the remote during the cricket. They work fine until the family grows, moves across three continents, and the cousins start arguing about what the rule actually was. Then somebody says: we should write this down. The Sikh panth reached that moment in the twentieth century, spread from Punjab to Malaya to California. Today: the written code.
screen: `RULES NOBODY WROTE DOWN.` → `THE FAMILY SPREADS OUT.` → `LET'S WRITE IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Rehat, from the start of this stretch, is the way a Sikh lives. Maryada means a boundary, a proper limit, the accepted way things are done. So Rehat Maryada is the agreed shape of a Sikh life. Codes of conduct weren't new. In the eighteenth century there were rahitnamas, manuals of conduct linked by tradition to the Guru's companions, and they didn't always agree. So in the 1930s, the SGPC, the elected body that runs the historic gurdwaras, gathered scholars and community leaders to draft one shared code. It took years of meetings and drafts. The panth agreed it in the 1940s, and it was published in 1950. It's short enough to read in an evening, and it has two halves. One is personal life: meditating on the Name, the daily prayers morning, evening and night, living by the Guru's teaching, honest work, sharing, service. The other is the community's life: how a gurdwara runs, how the Guru Granth Sahib is honored, the ceremonies for birth, naming, marriage and death, amrit, and how the panth decides things together. Everything in this stretch lives in it: kesh, kangha, kara, kachhera, kirpan, the four things avoided, the step of amrit, and yesterday's definition of a Sikh. The code isn't the Guru. For Sikhs, the Guru is the Guru Granth Sahib; the Rehat Maryada is the family agreement about how to live around the Guru. And it's shared. Some Sikh groups keep their own maryada alongside it, or instead. But a Sikh in Toronto and a Sikh in Amritsar can open the same short book and read the same words.
screen: `MARYADA — THE AGREED WAY, THE BOUNDARY.` · `OLDER RAHITNAMAS DIDN'T ALWAYS AGREE.` · `DRAFTED FOR YEARS, PUBLISHED IN 1950.` · `PERSONAL LIFE, AND THE COMMUNITY'S LIFE.` · then, large: `A SHARED CODE.`

segments.voice: Here's one line from the code, in plain words: a Sikh should earn by honest work, and share with others. Say it to yourself once, slowly, then think back over this stretch, from the hair kept to the open door, and hold whichever one stayed with you.
Rehat Maryada. The Sikh code of conduct: rehat, the way of living, and maryada, the agreed boundary. Drafted by the panth together, published in 1950.
Your line: a shared code. One agreement, kept together, around the Guru. See you tomorrow.
